issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, 'institutional failure' and especially 'betrayal by someone trusted' are hard to reconcile unless the crash involved unusual interpersonal circumstances not reflected anywhere else in the profile. The rest of the profile centers on fear/startle/intrusive sensory recall, which fits an accident trauma; these appraisal items instead imply an interpersonal or systemic-trauma narrative.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'Guilt on recall' can occur after accidents, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the chosen appraisal set: the appraisals focus on betrayal/institutional failure rather than self-blame or responsibility. That makes the guilt theme insufficiently supported across nodes for a coherent cognitive formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, the appraisal 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' is hard to reconcile unless the crash specifically involved a trusted driver or intentional wrongdoing, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere else in the profile. As presented, it introduces a different interpersonal-trauma theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' and 'Self-Blame' can sometimes coexist, but in this profile they point to different causal narratives for the trauma (trusted other's betrayal vs one's own actions causing the event) without any supporting context. That makes the appraisal set clinically hard to unify around a single MVC trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: The profile contains a hard-to-reconcile blame pattern: strong self-blame and guilt are paired with other-blame rumination as a core maladaptive strategy. Mixed blame can occur, but this combination is the main internal inconsistency in the selected items because the appraisals and memory items point toward inward blame, while the strategy item points toward sustained outward blame.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within the cognitive formulation, Maladaptive Strategies links most strongly to Negative Appraisals, so the strategy content should fit the appraisal style. Here the appraisal style is dominated by self-blame, helplessness, and permanent emotional damage, making other-blame rumination the least coherent strategy item.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, guilt on recall is plausible, especially with self-blame, so it is not problematic by itself. The concern is specifically its combination with persistent other-blame rumination, which pulls the profile toward a different blame direction than the rest of the formulation.

vignette:
The accident happened on a Tuesday evening in late October, just as the sun was setting. Carlos was driving home from a rehearsal at the community theater where he taught Afro-Cuban dance, his body still humming with the rhythm of the rumba he had been demonstrating. A pickup truck ran a red light and T-boned his sedan on the driver's side. The impact spun the car twice before it came to rest against a light pole. Carlos remembers the sound of tearing metal, the smell of gasoline, and the way his own voice sounded strange and distant when he tried to call out. He remembers the paramedic's gloved hand on his shoulder, and how he flinched so hard he nearly hit his head on the stretcher rail. That flinch has never really stopped. Now, eight months later, he reacts with alarm when his wife, Elena, touches his arm to get his attention at the dinner table, and he has come to believe that his body no longer belongs to him in the way it once did.

Carlos cannot put the event into words. When his doctor asked him to describe what happened, he found himself mute, his throat tight, the images flooding back without language. What comes to him instead are sounds: the screech of tires, the low groan of twisting metal, the sharp pop of the airbag deploying. These auditory fragments rise up without warning, often in the middle of a dance class when a student's sneaker squeaks against the floor or when the theater door slams shut. Each time they surface, he is flooded with a shame so acute it feels physical-a hot, crawling sensation under his skin. He has come to believe that the accident happened to him because of the sort of person he is: careless, distracted, someone who deserved to be punished. This conviction has taken root in him like a splinter he cannot remove. He is certain that he can never feel normal emotions again, that something essential inside him has been permanently shattered, and that no matter how carefully he lives, bad things will keep finding him because he is fundamentally the kind of person they happen to.

Because Carlos is convinced that catastrophe is always waiting, he has begun to scan for exits as soon as he enters any room or building. He does it automatically now-a quick, practiced sweep of the eyes that locates every door, every window, every possible escape route. The habit has become so ingrained that he cannot stop it, and the more he scans, the more vividly the memory of the crash returns: the blind panic of being trapped, the metal folding in around him, the certainty that he was about to die. Each memory reinforces his belief that he is helpless, that his character is flawed, that the world is a place where the next disaster is simply a matter of time. This loop tightens daily.

To manage the constant threat, Carlos has developed strategies that he knows, on some level, are not helping. He suppresses his thoughts about the trauma with tremendous effort, pushing them down the moment they surface, but the suppression itself seems to make the memories return more forcefully later, often as unbidden sounds or images that leave him disoriented and ashamed. He has also started staying up until very late, sometimes until three or four in the morning, because the hours before dawn feel safer-quieter, emptier, less likely to surprise him. The sleep deprivation leaves him exhausted and emotionally brittle, which in turn deepens his conviction that he is broken beyond repair. In the worst moments, he deliberately tries to leave his body, to blank out, to float somewhere above himself where the fear cannot reach him. But dissociation only fragments his memory further, making it harder to integrate what happened, and leaving him feeling more alienated from himself and from the life he used to lead.

The consequences have been concrete. Carlos has stopped teaching the advanced class because the dance studio has no back exit, only the single front door, and he cannot bear the trapped feeling that descends the moment he walks in. He now teaches only private lessons in a rented hall with four exits, and his income has dropped by nearly half. Elena has noticed that he no longer dances at home, that he flinches from her touch, that he spends his evenings staring at the ceiling instead of sleeping beside her. She asked him last week if he was angry with her, and he could not find the words to explain that he is not angry-he is terrified, and ashamed of being terrified, and convinced that he is no longer the man she married.

What finally brought Carlos to seek help was a moment in the grocery store last Tuesday. A child dropped a jar of pasta sauce, and the sound of glass shattering sent him to his knees in the aisle, his hands over his ears, his heart slamming against his ribs. A stranger helped him up. He could not stop apologizing. He is afraid that next time, he will not be able to get back up at all. He is hoping, more than he can say, that someone can help him find a way back into his own body, into his own life, before the man he used to be disappears entirely.
